crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: High-Frequency Market Microstructure
children.blurb: High-frequency market microstructure is the study of how prices form and orders execute at very short time scales, from milliseconds to seconds.

children.name: Non-Linear Factor Models
children.blurb: Non-linear factor models are quantitative return models in which the relationship between a stock's return and its underlying factors is not assumed to be a straight line.

children.name: Learning Trade Execution
children.blurb: Learning trade execution covers the methods that decide how an order actually reaches the market: when to send it, in what size, through which venue, and at what price limit.

children.name: Statistical Arbitrage
children.blurb: Statistical arbitrage is a family of quantitative trading strategies that look for small, repeatable price relationships between related instruments and trade on the expectation that those relationships revert.

children.name: Detecting Market Regime Shifts
children.blurb: Detecting market regime shifts is the practice of identifying when the statistical character of a market changes, for example from calm trending conditions to volatile mean-reverting ones.

sections.body: Quantitative trading applies statistical and machine learning methods to financial markets, turning prices, order books, and alternative data into signals and execution decisions. In practice, AI now forecasts short-term price moves, estimates optimal trade timing, and detects shifts in market behavior. High-frequency systems use deep learning on order book events to predict microprice changes. Factor models use neural networks to capture nonlinear relationships among stocks. Execution algorithms learn to slice orders and minimize market impact. Statistical arbitrage strategies scan thousands of instruments for temporary mispricings.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The field is mature in execution and short-horizon prediction, where models are retrained frequently and evaluated on live data. What is solved includes basic market making, volume-weighted average price execution, and linear factor risk models. What is not solved includes robust regime change detection, long-horizon alpha, and avoiding overfitting to historical noise. Honest limits are severe: non-stationarity, low signal-to-noise ratios, and the fact that a profitable strategy decays once others adopt it. Backtests often fail live because of costs, latency, and crowding. No model reliably predicts crashes or turns.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages here cover distinct layers of the trading stack. High-Frequency Market Microstructure explains the data and mechanics at the shortest timescales, which matters for anyone building execution or market making systems. Non-Linear Factor Models covers cross-sectional return prediction, where the goal is ranking assets rather than timing trades. Learning Trade Execution focuses on the action side, how to place orders to reduce cost and slippage. Statistical Arbitrage ties prediction and execution together into relative value strategies that bet on convergence. Detecting Market Regime Shifts addresses the hardest problem, knowing when the statistical rules have changed so that models can be paused or retrained. A reader would go to microstructure for foundations, factor models for stock selection, execution for implementation, statistical arbitrage for strategy design, and regime shifts for risk control.
